episode_title: Dr. Barry Davis on Emotional Intelligence, Program Building, and Leading Calmly as a Coach
question: How did Dr. Barry Davis transition from his first head coaching job at Gloucester County College to Ryder University, and what enabled him to win three conference championships and reach three regionals in six years?
transcript_excerpt: After 11 years at Gloucester County College where he won four national championships in Division III, Davis moved to an NAIA school in Georgia for four years. He then applied for the Ryder University Division I position with help from good connections. Once at Ryder, Davis credits his success to staying calm, being interested in people, providing a safe environment for players to talk, empowering assistant coaches and players with input, and shifting his focus from winning to teaching and setting an example. This approach led to three conference championships and three regionals appearances in six years, including knocking off a number one seed at their place in front of 5,000 people.

episode_title: Dr. Barry Davis on Emotional Intelligence, Program Building, and Leading Calmly as a Coach
question: What specific moment caused Dr. Barry Davis to realize he needed to develop emotional intelligence as a coach, and what was his lowest point in leadership?
transcript_excerpt: Davis's lowest point was an incident on the New Jersey Turnpike around 1990 when he made his players run down the highway shoulder after a piece of ice hit him during a team drive. He did not recognize this as wrong at the time, and it took years before he realized his mistake. Three significant moments changed his coaching philosophy: receiving an audio cassette from football coach Tony Mason, meeting baseball coach Skip Bertman at LSU, and hearing a 2007 speech by Pat Williams, the executive vice president of the Orlando Magic, on his seven sides of leadership. Pat Williams's speech on people skills was particularly transformative, and when combined with his PhD research beginning in 2014 on what great leaders and coaches do consistently, Davis began to systematically work on emotional intelligence.

episode_title: Dr. Barry Davis on Emotional Intelligence, Program Building, and Leading Calmly as a Coach
question: What is the 'self-talk walk' technique that Dr. Barry Davis invented to maintain emotional control and leadership presence during practice?
transcript_excerpt: Davis invented the self-talk walk where he would walk to practice and talk to himself, saying: 'Be patient, be steady, be calm, don't ever be shook, be the teacher, be the leader, set the example.' As he reached the fence and gate to the practice field, his mindset would align with staying calm, teaching, leading, and setting an example. He did this consistently and found that when players made mistakes, instead of flipping out as he would have 25 years earlier, he stayed calmer and more leadership-like. Players became more comfortable and looked to him waiting for him to blow up, but he didn't, creating a safer environment for learning.

episode_title: Dr. Barry Davis on Emotional Intelligence, Program Building, and Leading Calmly as a Coach
question: How did Dr. Barry Davis's coaching philosophy and approach to player development differ between his early career and his final years before retirement at Ryder University?
transcript_excerpt: In his early career as a 24-year-old head coach at Gloucester County College, Davis was influenced by coaches like Bobby Knight and Woody Hayes, adopting an authoritative, tough persona and being quick to anger—even when winning four national championships. However, in the last 10 years of his career before retiring in 2025, he was significantly more successful because he paid attention to people skills and emotional intelligence. He shifted from 'I'm going to practice with mine. The games are yours' to truly teaching and modeling self-discipline. He became vulnerable, empowered assistant coaches and players to have input, invited one-on-one conversations about coaching preferences, asked players for solutions before giving advice, and held meetings while walking in the outfield rather than locked in his office. Former players who played for him early in his career expressed disbelief at how he had changed.

question: What are the core pillars of Dr. Barry Davis's leadership framework outlined in his book 'Old Dog, New Tricks'?
transcript_excerpt: Dr. Davis mentions five main pillars in his program-building and coaching framework, with emotional intelligence serving as the sixth pillar. While the transcription does not explicitly list all five original pillars by name, Davis references his leadership approach as being 'authentic, committed, and confident' while 'modeling self-discipline that tries to produce excellence in myself and in other people.' His framework emphasizes remaining calm, being interested in others, providing a safe environment for communication, intentionally and consistently creating space for players to talk and listen, giving up some power to empower others, and shifting focus from winning to teaching and setting an example—all principles detailed in his book 'Old Dog, New Tricks: The Power of Leading with Emotional Intelligence.'
